title: Forgive our mistakes
hookLine: the Ardas asks forgiveness for any letter added or missed, any slip in the reading

cards: A family has just heard the whole Guru Granth Sahib read aloud. That's an akhand paath: one unbroken reading, day and night, the readers taking turns while the house sleeps. At the end, the family stands for the Ardas.
And somewhere in it comes a request that sounds almost like a proofreader's note. Forgive any letter added. Forgive any letter missed.
Forgive every slip. After all that care, the readers still ask pardon for the mistakes.

teach.b: The Punjabi phrase is akhar vaadha ghaata bhul chuk maaf karni. Akhar is a letter, a syllable. Vaadha is something added, ghaata something left out.
Bhul is a mistake that comes from forgetting or not knowing. Chuk is a slip, a miss. Maaf karni: please forgive.

It's said after a reading, a recitation, a kirtan, any time the words of the Guru have passed through human mouths. Why would a letter matter so much? Because for Sikhs the Guru Granth Sahib isn't a book about the Guru.
It is the Guru, the living teacher in words. Reading it is something like speaking in the Guru's own voice, and care with every syllable is a form of respect. But the line isn't anxious.
It doesn't promise the reading was perfect; it assumes it wasn't.

Guru Nanak said as much in Sri Rag, on ang 61: everyone makes mistakes; only the Guru and the Creator never do. That's not an insult to the readers. It's just the truth about people, said without drama.

teach.h: DO YOUR BEST, THEN ASK PARDON.
teach.b: So the Ardas builds an apology into its own structure: the best care a reader can give, an admission that it probably fell short, then letting it go.
A reader who had to be perfect might never open the book. A reader who knows the pardon is already part of the prayer can stand up, open it, and begin.
And the request is made for everyone who read, so it covers every reader's slips, not one person's.

how: After a reading or recitation, the Ardas includes akhar vaadha ghaata bhul chuk maaf karni, asking forgiveness for any syllable added or missed and any error in the reading.

o: mistakes and slips, asked to be forgiven
a careful reading with no errors at all
a letter added to make the reading longer

games.q: forgive our mistakes — tap the pairs.

s: the Ardas claims the reading was perfect
it assumes mistakes happened and asks pardon for them.
Guru Nanak says everyone makes mistakes except the Guru and the Creator
an akhand paath reads the Guru Granth Sahib straight through
one unbroken reading, readers taking turns through the night.

games.q: you've just finished an unbroken reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib. the Ardas begins. what's asked?
o: forgiveness for any letter added or missed.
nothing about the reading at all.
games.why: akhar vaadha ghaata bhul chuk maaf karni: after all that care, the Ardas still asks pardon for the slips.

practice: Think back over the last day or two and let one small slip come up, a sharp word, a forgotten text, a promise that slid; one is enough.
Notice how it feels in your body, then picture saying sorry to that person in a single plain sentence, no excuses attached. If you pray, ask the One to forgive the errors, yours and theirs.

wordCard.voice: Bhul chuk, mistake and slip: the Ardas asks pardon for them, akhar vaadha ghaata bhul chuk maaf karni, any letter added or missed, any error at all.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a mistake from forgetting, and a slip; said together, any error at all.

carryVoice: Your line: forgive the errors. Best care first, then pardon, then begin again. See you tomorrow.
